text: Every lesson in Chapter four ended with a specific rejection scenario. Chapter five steps back and organizes what those scenarios have in common — a clear model for where validation happens, and why "rejected" is not one single kind of failure.

Validation happens in two layers. Load-time validation, when Load Interface File for Import reads your file, only checks that it's a structurally valid CSV — no concept of a supplier existing or an account balancing. Import-time validation, when the product-specific import process runs, applies the real business rules: does this supplier exist, do lines sum to the header, does this account combination exist, do debits equal credits.

A file can sail through load-time validation with zero issues and still generate dozens of import-time rejections — exactly the pattern you saw across chapter four. Knowing which layer you're in tells you where to look: a load-time failure means something's wrong with the file itself; an import-time rejection means something's wrong with one row's business content, which you can usually trace and fix without touching the file structure.

A rejected row with a recorded reason is a far better outcome than one that just vanishes. AP_INTERFACE_REJECTIONS, an AutoInvoice exception, a Mass Additions review queue — all exist so a failed row leaves a trail. The system is doing its job when it rejects bad data loudly. The trouble only starts if that detail goes unread.

Start with the execution report for a first read of what failed; if that's not specific enough, query the interface table and its rejections structure directly. Nearly every rejection traces back to one of the specific causes named across chapter four. Up next, lesson twenty-one: correcting and re-running the imports that produced them.
